screens.title: Variables, Data Types, and User Input in C
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how programs remember information. Variables are simply named boxes in memory where we store data. You will learn how to declare and initialize these boxes, choose the correct data type so the compiler knows how much space to set aside, and how to display and read values from the console. We’ll walk through integers, floating-point numbers, characters, and boolean types. You will also see how the print function uses format placeholders to interpret values correctly, and how the user-input function needs the address of a variable to write into that box. We’ll practice basic arithmetic and highlight a subtle but common trap: integer division truncates fractional parts unless you explicitly use or cast to a floating type. By the end you’ll be able to write small interactive programs that prompt the user, accept input, and compute results without crashing. Think of this chapter as learning how to name, label, and safely use the boxes where your program keeps its information.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Variables & Input
Variables, Data Types, and User Input in C
Store, display, and accept data safely from the user using C's core primitives.
In this lesson

How to declare and initialize variables, choose between int, float, double, char, and bool, print and read values using format specifiers, and perform arithmetic while avoiding common traps.

Why this matters
Programs that store and transform input are the backbone of interactive software — from CLI tools to full applications. Correct types and I/O prevent crashes and incorrect results.
Explore Key Topics
Types & Memory
How the choice of type affects storage and precision.
I/O with printf/scanf
Format specifiers and the address-of operator for input.
Arithmetic & Casting
Integer division vs floating-point results and how to cast to get the right output.
Visual Concept
Named Memory Boxes
Each variable name labels a box. The type decides box size and what you can store.
int
age
float
price
char
c
Address-of for Input
Giving scanf the variable's address is like handing someone the location of the box so they can put the value inside.
Key Takeaway

Declare variables with the right type, print with matching format specifiers, and pass addresses to scanf to read input safely.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives are designed to move you from seeing output to building interactive programs. First, you will be able to declare and initialize variables in C so your program can store values with meaningful names. That skill matters because every piece of data in a program must live somewhere. Second, you will learn the common C data types—int, float, double, char, and bool—so you can choose the correct representation and avoid precision or range errors. Third, you will practice using the print function with the correct format specifiers so values appear as expected; wrong specifiers lead to confusing output. Fourth, you will obtain user input using the standard input function and understand why the address-of operator is required. Each objective has a short verification milestone to confirm competency. Throughout, expect concrete examples and short exercises that demonstrate these abilities so you can confidently build small interactive programs.

screens.title: What is a Variable?
screens.narratorSegment: A variable is simply a named storage location in your program's memory. When you declare a variable in C, you tell the compiler the name and the type, which determines how much memory is reserved and how the bits are interpreted. Think of declaring int counter; as creating a labeled box named counter that will hold whole numbers. Initializing a variable gives that box a starting value, for example int counter = 1; which places the number one into the labeled box immediately. This distinction matters because uninitialized variables can contain garbage values and lead to unpredictable behavior. A helpful concrete example: if you declare float temperature; and then attempt to print it without initializing, you might see a meaningless number. A common misconception is believing variables are just names; in C they are typed and sized. Another confusion is assuming initialization always happens automatically — it does not. Key takeaway: always declare with the correct type and initialize when you need a defined starting state. How would you name the variables in a program that records a user's age and grade?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › What is a Variable?
Definition & analogy

Think of variables as labeled boxes in memory. The type on declaration decides how big each box is and what can be stored inside.

Analogy
Label the box "age" and put the number 30 inside. The label makes it easy to find and use later.
Common mistake
Assuming an uninitialized variable contains zero. In C it contains whatever bits were present unless you initialize it.
Key Takeaway

Declare with a type and initialize to define a starting value; otherwise expect unpredictable contents.

Concrete example
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
  int age = 30;      // a named integer box with initial value 30
  char initial = 'A'; // a char box holding a single character
  printf("Age: %i
Initial: %c
", age, initial);
  return 0;
}
Run this to confirm the boxes contain the expected values. If age were not initialized, printing could show an unexpected number.

screens.title: Declaring and Initializing Variables
screens.narratorSegment: Declaring and initializing are two related but distinct actions. Declaration tells the compiler the variable's name and type so it can reserve memory. Initialization assigns an initial value at the point of declaration. For example, int score; declares a box; int score = 100; both declares and initializes it. You will practice both because leaving a variable uninitialized is a frequent source of bugs. Notice naming rules: start with a letter or underscore, use letters, numbers, and underscores only, and choose clear names like student_id or average_score. Also be aware that float literals need an f suffix when you want a float rather than a double. As a concrete example, declaring float price = 9.99f ensures the literal is treated as single precision. A common misconception is that initialization is optional and safe; in many cases it is not. Key practice: initialize variables when you need a known starting state and prefer meaningful names. Try naming and initializing three different variables and printing them to verify the contents. Declaring and Initializing Variables means declare with the type first, initialize with = value, use clear names, and add f for float literals when needed.. In practical terms, syntax rules, examples, and safe initialization habits in c.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Declaring & Initializing
Rules & best practices
  • Write the type, then the name, then optionally = initial value, then semicolon.
  • Use meaningful names like student_id or average_score.
  • Initialize when you need a known start to avoid garbage values.
Common pitfall
Forgetting the f suffix for float literals can lead the literal to be treated as double in some contexts; be explicit when you need single precision.
Try this

Declare and initialize three variables of different types, then print them to confirm values match expectations.

Code example
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
  int score = 100;
  float price = 9.99f; // 'f' suffix for float literal
  char grade = 'A';
  printf("Score: %i
Price: %.2f
Grade: %c
", score, price, grade);
  return 0;
}
Observe that each variable was both declared and initialized. Run and confirm that price prints with two decimal places using %.2f.

screens.title: Fundamental Data Types in C
screens.narratorSegment: C provides a small set of fundamental data types that cover most simple programming needs. The integer type stores whole numbers and is appropriate for counts, indexes, and identifiers. Floating-point types come in two common flavors: float for single precision and double for double precision; use double when you need more accuracy or range. The char type stores a single character: it’s ideal for letters, digits, or punctuation represented by one symbol. Booleans are available through the boolean header and represent true or false states—useful for flags and conditions. A concrete example: use int for a user's age, double for a precise average score, char for a grade letter, and bool for a game_over flag. A misconception is treating float and double interchangeably — doubles provide more precision and are generally preferred for calculations that require accuracy. Also be mindful of size limits; very large integers may overflow. Key practice: choose the smallest type that safely represents your data but prefer double for decimal math unless memory is constrained. Fundamental Data Types in C means pick int for whole values, double for most decimal math, char for single characters, and bool for logical states.. In practical terms, int, float, double, char, and bool — when and why to use each.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Data Types
Type hierarchy & usage
int
Whole numbers like counts, indices, or IDs. Example: int age = 21;
float
Single precision decimals. Example: float temp = 36.6f;
double
Double precision decimals for accuracy. Example: double pi = 3.14159;
char
Single character in single quotes. Example: char grade = 'A';
bool (from stdbool.h)
Stores true or false for logical conditions. Example: bool is_active = true;
Misconception

Assuming float precision is always enough. For many calculations, double is the safer default to avoid rounding errors.

Quick examples
int count = 10;
double average = 87.256;
char initial = 'Z';
bool done = false;
Use these small snippets to test printing and behavior in short programs.

screens.title: Printing with printf and Format Specifiers
screens.narratorSegment: Printing values requires telling the print facility what type to expect. The format string contains placeholders that correspond to each value in order. For integers use the integer placeholder, for characters use the character placeholder, and for decimal numbers use the floating placeholder with optional precision control. A concrete example: printing a student's id, average score, and grade letter requires a format like string with integer, floating, and character placeholders in the same order as you supply the variables. A common mistake is mismatching the placeholder and the variable type, which can produce incorrect output or runtime warnings. For doubles, note that the printing placeholder for decimal numbers works with both float and double, but when reading input there is a difference. Use precision specifiers such as two decimals to make numeric output readable. Practice by formatting a mix of int, double, and char and observing how changing precision affects the displayed numbers. Closing question: how would you format a currency value with two decimals? Printing with printf and Format Specifiers means match each placeholder to the variable's type and supply variables in the same order as placeholders appear.. In practical terms, tell the print function how to interpret each variable so output is correct and readable.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Printf & Specifiers
Specifiers to remember
  • %i or %d for integers.
  • %f for floating-point numbers; use format like %.2f for two decimals.
  • %c for single characters; %s for strings (covered later).
Common confusion
Using the wrong specifier will not convert the value; it tells the print function how to interpret the bits you pass.
Key Takeaway

Always align placeholders with variable types and pass variables in the precise order to avoid incorrect output.

Example code
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
  int id = 12345;
  double avg = 87.45678;
  char grade = 'B';
  printf("ID: %i
Average: %.2f
Grade: %c
", id, avg, grade);
  return 0;
}
This prints the average with two decimals. Try changing %.2f to %.1f to see the effect on rounding and readability.

screens.title: Reading Input with scanf and the Address-of Operator
screens.narratorSegment: To accept input from the user, C provides a formatted input function that reads from the standard input and stores values in variables you supply. The important detail is that scanf needs the memory address of the variable so it can place the characters it reads into that location. The address-of operator returns that address; for an integer variable named number you call the input function with the integer placeholder and ampersand number. A concrete analogy: if a friend needs to put a book into a labeled box, you must hand them the box's address, not the book currently inside. A common beginner error is omitting the address-of operator; then the input function interprets whatever happens to be stored in the variable as an address and tries to write there, often causing a crash. Practice by writing a short program that asks for a number and prints it. Then deliberately omit the address-of to observe the error and restore the ampersand to fix it. Always validate input in larger programs to avoid unsafe behavior. Reading Input with scanf and the Address-of Operator means pass the variable's address to scanf so it can store input in the correct memory location; omitting & leads to undefined behavior.. In practical terms, how scanf writes user input into your variables' memory locations.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › scanf & Address-of
How it works
scanf reads formatted input and stores it at the memory address you provide. The address-of operator gives that address. Without it, scanf does not know where to put the input.
Analogy
Handing a delivery driver the box's address so they can put the package inside, rather than giving them the package and expecting them to find the box.
Warning

Forgetting the address-of operator often leads to a segmentation fault because the function tries to write to an invalid address.

Code example
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
  int user_age;
  printf("Please enter your age: ");
  scanf("%i", &user_age); // '&' gives scanf the address to store the value
  printf("You are %i years old.
", user_age);
  return 0;
}
Run this and enter a number to observe successful input storage. Then try removing & to see the runtime error and understand why the address is required.

screens.title: Correct vs Incorrect scanf Usage
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing correct and incorrect usage of the input function illustrates the danger of missing the address-of operator. Correct usage provides the address so the function knows where to store the incoming data. Incorrect usage passes the current value of the variable, which is not an address, and leads to undefined behavior such as crashes. For example, calling the input function with the placeholder and ampersand on an integer variable safely writes the typed number into that variable. If you omit the ampersand, the input function treats the value contained in the uninitialized variable as an address to write to. That usually points to memory the program cannot access, producing a segmentation fault. Beginners sometimes mistake the ampersand for an operator they only need for special cases, but with scanf it is required for basic types. Practice by writing the correct form, then intentionally run the incorrect form in a controlled environment to see the failure. The safe habit is always to include the address-of when reading standard types with scanf. Correct vs Incorrect scanf Usage means always pass the address of variables to scanf; omitting & typically causes undefined behavior and crashes.. In practical terms, compare a safe input call with the common faulty call that omits the address-of operator.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › scanf: Correct vs Incorrect
Correct
int value;
scanf("%i", &value); // address provided
printf("Value: %i
", value);
This form safely writes the input into the variable's memory location.
Incorrect

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Arithmetic Operators
Operator list
  • Addition: +
  • Subtraction: -
  • Multiplication: *
  • Division: / (integer or floating behavior depends on operand types)
  • Modulo: % (remainder of integer division)
Pitfall
Integer division truncates the decimal. To get a decimal result, cast at least one operand to float or use float literals.
Key Takeaway

To preserve fractional parts, operate with floating-point numbers or cast integers before division.

Example calculations
int a = 10;
int b = 3;
printf("Sum: %i
", a + b);         // 13
printf("Quotient (int): %i
", a / b); // 3
printf("Remainder: %i
", a % b);    // 1
printf("Quotient (float): %.2f
", (float)a / b); // 3.33
Try casting only one operand to see the difference in division results and confirm the printed decimal places match expectations.

screens.title: Integer Division vs Floating-point Division
screens.narratorSegment: Integer division occurs when both operands are integers: the division produces an integer quotient and discards any fractional remainder. For example, dividing ten by three with integer operands yields three, not 3.33. In contrast, floating-point division yields a decimal result when one or both operands are floats or doubles. The practical implication is that if you write expressions with integer variables expecting fractional precision, you will be surprised by truncated results. The solution is to use floating types or to cast operands explicitly to float or double in the expression. A concrete example is converting one integer to float using a cast and then performing the division to receive a fractional result that you can format and print. A common misconception is that the division operation itself decides whether to include decimals; actually the types of the operands determine the result type. Checklist for safer code

  • Initialize variables to sensible defaults to avoid garbage values.

Small code guard

  printf("Invalid input
");
  return 1;
}
This simple check makes the program more robust when users enter unexpected text.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's consolidate the most important points. First, variables are named storage locations whose type you declare up front; initialization gives them a defined starting value. Second, choose types intentionally: use int for whole numbers, double for most decimal calculations, char for individual characters, and bool for logical flags when you include the boolean header. Third, printing requires matching format specifiers so the runtime interprets values correctly. Fourth, when reading input you must pass the address of the variable so the input function can store the value at that location; omitting the address causes undefined behavior. Finally, remember arithmetic rules: integer division truncates decimals, so cast to floating types when you need fractional results. These rules form the foundation of safe, predictable C programs and help you avoid the most common beginner errors.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how programs remember information. Variables are simply named boxes in memory where we store data. You will learn how to declare and initialize these boxes, choose the correct data type so the compiler knows how much space to set aside, and how to display and read values from the console. We’ll walk through integers, floating-point numbers, characters, and boolean types. You will also see how the print function uses format placeholders to interpret values correctly, and how the user-input function needs the address of a variable to write into that box. We’ll practice basic arithmetic and highlight a subtle but common trap: integer division truncates fractional parts unless you explicitly use or cast to a floating type. By the end you’ll be able to write small interactive programs that prompt the user, accept input, and compute results without crashing. Think of this chapter as learning how to name, label, and safely use the boxes where your program keeps its information.

These objectives are designed to move you from seeing output to building interactive programs. First, you will be able to declare and initialize variables in C so your program can store values with meaningful names. That skill matters because every piece of data in a program must live somewhere. Second, you will learn the common C data types—int, float, double, char, and bool—so you can choose the correct representation and avoid precision or range errors. Third, you will practice using the print function with the correct format specifiers so values appear as expected; wrong specifiers lead to confusing output. Fourth, you will obtain user input using the standard input function and understand why the address-of operator is required. Each objective has a short verification milestone to confirm competency. Throughout, expect concrete examples and short exercises that demonstrate these abilities so you can confidently build small interactive programs.

This second objectives screen expands each skill into a practical milestone so you know when you have reached competency. For declarations and initialization, you will create variables such as int count = 0 and confirm they hold expected values when printed. For data types, practice choosing int for counts, float or double for measured values like temperature, char for single characters, and include the boolean header to use true or false. For printing, practice format specifiers with examples like printing an integer with the integer placeholder and a float with two decimals. For input, run short programs that call the input function and deliberately try leaving out the address-of to observe the error and then correct it. Each card includes a small mnemonic: name the box, pick the right size, tell the printer what it is, and give the reader the address. These habits reduce runtime errors and make debugging faster.

A variable is simply a named storage location in your program's memory. When you declare a variable in C, you tell the compiler the name and the type, which determines how much memory is reserved and how the bits are interpreted. Think of declaring int counter; as creating a labeled box named counter that will hold whole numbers. Initializing a variable gives that box a starting value, for example int counter = 1; which places the number one into the labeled box immediately. This distinction matters because uninitialized variables can contain garbage values and lead to unpredictable behavior. A helpful concrete example: if you declare float temperature; and then attempt to print it without initializing, you might see a meaningless number. A common misconception is believing variables are just names; in C they are typed and sized. Another confusion is assuming initialization always happens automatically — it does not. Key takeaway: always declare with the correct type and initialize when you need a defined starting state. How would you name the variables in a program that records a user's age and grade?

Declaring and initializing are two related but distinct actions. Declaration tells the compiler the variable's name and type so it can reserve memory. Initialization assigns an initial value at the point of declaration. For example, int score; declares a box; int score = 100; both declares and initializes it. You will practice both because leaving a variable uninitialized is a frequent source of bugs. Notice naming rules: start with a letter or underscore, use letters, numbers, and underscores only, and choose clear names like student_id or average_score. Also be aware that float literals need an f suffix when you want a float rather than a double. As a concrete example, declaring float price = 9.99f ensures the literal is treated as single precision. A common misconception is that initialization is optional and safe; in many cases it is not. Key practice: initialize variables when you need a known starting state and prefer meaningful names. Try naming and initializing three different variables and printing them to verify the contents. Declaring and Initializing Variables means declare with the type first, initialize with = value, use clear names, and add f for float literals when needed.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

C provides a small set of fundamental data types that cover most simple programming needs. The integer type stores whole numbers and is appropriate for counts, indexes, and identifiers. Floating-point types come in two common flavors: float for single precision and double for double precision; use double when you need more accuracy or range. The char type stores a single character: it’s ideal for letters, digits, or punctuation represented by one symbol. Booleans are available through the boolean header and represent true or false states—useful for flags and conditions. A concrete example: use int for a user's age, double for a precise average score, char for a grade letter, and bool for a game_over flag. A misconception is treating float and double interchangeably — doubles provide more precision and are generally preferred for calculations that require accuracy. Also be mindful of size limits; very large integers may overflow. Key practice: choose the smallest type that safely represents your data but prefer double for decimal math unless memory is constrained. Printing values requires telling the print facility what type to expect. The format string contains placeholders that correspond to each value in order. For integers use the integer placeholder, for characters use the character placeholder, and for decimal numbers use the floating placeholder with optional precision control. Let's consolidate the most important points. First, variables are named storage locations whose type you declare up front; initialization gives them a defined starting value. Second, choose types intentionally: use int for whole numbers, double for most decimal calculations, char for individual characters, and bool for logical flags when you include the boolean header. Third, printing requires matching format specifiers so the runtime interprets values correctly. Fourth, when reading input you must pass the address of the variable so the input function can store the value at that location; omitting the address causes undefined behavior. Finally, remember arithmetic rules: integer division truncates decimals, so cast to floating types when you need fractional results.
